# Configuration reference

<!-- GENERATED by scripts/gen-reference.py from crates/mesh-core/src/config.rs. Do not edit by hand; CI fails when this file is stale. -->

Every key a node's `meshnode.toml` accepts. The file is optional, and so is every key in it:
a node with no file runs on defaults, and that is how most nodes run.

| | Where the file is |
|---|---|
| A node you started with `meshnode up` | `~/.meshware/meshnode.toml`, or `$MESHWARE_HOME/meshnode.toml` |
| A packaged node (`.deb`, `.rpm`, `meshnode adopt`) | `/etc/meshware/meshnode.toml` |
| The node Director drives | `~/.meshware/meshnode.toml` — the same file, since Director runs no node of its own |

**An unknown key is refused**, at every level, rather than ignored: a misspelling would
otherwise be a setting that silently does nothing. Check a file before a node reads it:

```console
$ meshnode config check              # parse and validate this node's file
$ meshnode config show               # the configuration after flags, environment and defaults
$ meshnode config paths              # every path the node uses
```

**Precedence**, highest first: a command-line flag, then an environment variable
([environment reference](environment.md)), then this file, then the default.

**Reloading.** `systemctl reload meshnode` (or `SIGHUP`) applies the keys marked *reloads*
below while the node keeps running; the node logs what it applied and names anything that
needs a restart. Keys marked *restart* take effect the next time the node starts.

## Top-level keys

Outside any table, at the top of the file.

- **`node_name`** · string · *restart*

  This machine's name in the mesh, as `meshnode nodes` and Director show it. Default: the hostname.

- **`data_dir`** · path · *restart*

  Where the heavy directories (state, jobs, content) live, when they belong on a different volume from the config. Default: the home itself. The home is chosen by `--data-dir` or `$MESHWARE_HOME`, never by this key: the file lives inside it.

- **`tags`** · list of strings · *reloads*

  Tags this node announces for itself, which selectors, grants and placement match on: `["gpu", "dc=east"]`. Tags an admin assigns from anywhere (`meshnode nodes tag`) are kept separately and survive a rebuild; these are rewritten from this file at every start.

## [listen]

<a id="listen"></a>

`[listen]` — where this node accepts mesh traffic: QUIC, over UDP.

- **`addr`** · string · *restart*

  The address to bind. Default `0.0.0.0`, every IPv4 interface. Write an IPv6 address in brackets — `"[::]"` serves both families on a dual-stack host — because it is joined to the port as `addr:port`. A specific address is also the only one the node advertises.

- **`port`** · integer · *restart*

  The UDP port. Default 7777, the one port every member must be able to reach on every other.

## [mesh]

<a id="mesh"></a>

`[mesh]` — the mesh this node founds, if it founds one.

- **`name`** · string · *used once, when this node founds a mesh*

  Name used when this node bootstraps a brand-new mesh. Ignored once a genesis document exists.

## [log]

<a id="log"></a>

`[log]` — how much the daemon logs, and where.

- **`level`** · string · *reloads*

  `error`, `warn`, `info` (default), `debug` or `trace` — or a full filter such as `info,mesh_core::gossip=debug`. `$MESHWARE_LOG` overrides it, and `$RUST_LOG`, when set, overrides both.

- **`format`** · string · *restart*

  `text` (default) or `json` (structured logs for shippers).

- **`dir`** · path · *restart*

  When set, the daemon logs to `<dir>/meshnode.log` with built-in size-based rotation instead of stderr.

  A **relative** path is resolved under the home, so `dir = "logs"` means `<home>/logs` — which is the one place logs should go if they are going anywhere. An absolute path is honoured as given, for the operator who wants them on a separate volume.

- **`max_size_mb`** · integer · *restart*

  Rotate the log file once it exceeds this size (default 20 MB).

- **`max_files`** · integer · *restart*

  Rotated files kept (`meshnode.log.1` … `.N`, default 5).

## [secrets]

<a id="secrets"></a>

`[secrets.providers.<name>]` — external secret provider plugins. The plugin contract: `plugin get`, JSON `{path,key,config}` on stdin, `{"value":…}` on stdout.

Each provider is its own table, named for the provider:

```toml
[secrets.providers.vault]
plugin = "/usr/local/libexec/meshware-vault"
config = { addr = "https://vault.internal:8200" }
```

- **`plugin`** · string · *reloads*

  Path to the provider plugin executable.

- **`config`** · toml::Table · *reloads*

  Arbitrary provider configuration, passed to the plugin verbatim.

## [limits]

<a id="limits"></a>

`[limits]` — caps on the capacity-derived defaults. By default the node is greedy: slots = CPU cores, queue = 4 × slots.

- **`slots`** · integer · *reloads*

  Concurrent executor slots. Absent/0 = derive from hardware.

- **`queue`** · integer · *reloads*

  Pending queue depth. Absent = 4 × slots (min 8).

- **`min_free_mem_mb`** · integer · *reloads*

  Memory admission floor: queued jobs are not promoted into slots while `MemAvailable` is below this. Absent = 256 MB; 0 disables the gate.

- **`quiet`** · string, or list of strings · *reloads*

  Quiet hours: time-boxed caps on `slots`, in this machine's own local time (`crate::quiet`).

  ```toml quiet = "08:00-23:00 @ 30%" quiet = ["00:00-08:00 @ 100%", "08:00-23:00 @ 30%"] ```

  Absent = no quiet hours, which is what every node did before this existed and what a machine in a rack should keep doing.

## [http]

<a id="http"></a>

`[http]` — the local observability endpoint: `GET /healthz` and `GET /metrics` (Prometheus) on every node.

- **`enabled`** · boolean · *restart*

  Default true. The endpoint is loopback-only by default; disabling it removes the listener entirely.

- **`addr`** · string · *restart*

  Default `127.0.0.1:7776`. Port 0 = kernel-assigned (tests).

## [api]

<a id="api"></a>

`[api]` — the HTTP API. **Off unless `listen` is set.**

Deliberately a second listener rather than a route on `[http]`: that one serves `/healthz` and `/metrics` unauthenticated by design, and sharing a port would mean exposing the API to a network silently exposed the metrics too.

The API is plain HTTP and every request is a *signed envelope*, so a network attacker cannot forge one — only read a response. Put a reverse proxy in front of it if it needs to leave the host.

- **`listen`** · string · *restart*

  e.g. `127.0.0.1:7778`. Unset means no listener at all.

## [retention]

<a id="retention"></a>

`[retention]` — how long this node keeps finished jobs' files and unused content, and how much of them.

- **`job_days`** · integer · *reloads*

  Terminal jobs older than this many days are pruned. 0 = keep forever.

- **`job_max_mb`** · integer · *reloads*

  Total size cap for job history in MB; oldest terminal jobs are pruned first. 0 = unlimited.

- **`content`** · string · *reloads*

  How hard this node tidies its content store: `keep`, `relaxed`, `balanced` (the default), `tidy`, `lean`, `ephemeral`.

  A level rather than a number, because the decision is a posture and the day count is how it is implemented — see [`mesh_proto::ContentPolicy`]. An operator who wants the number writes `content_days` instead; both go through the mesh policy, and neither can keep *more* than the mesh allows.

- **`content_days`** · integer · *reloads*

  The window in days, for an operator who would rather say `45` than pick a rung. Wins over `content` when both are set.

- **`content_max_mb`** · integer · *reloads*

  Total size cap for the content store in MB; the coldest unreferenced bundles go first. 0 = no cap, and the `[disk]` floor is then the only thing bounding it.

## [wan]

<a id="wan"></a>

`[wan]` — WAN reachability: manually advertised public endpoints, whether this node relays for NATed peers, and whether a NATed node may use relays. Everything here is hot-reloadable (SIGHUP).

- **`advertise`** · list of strings · *reloads*

  Extra `host:port` endpoints this node is reachable on (a cloud VM's elastic IP, a port-forward). Announced as direct candidates and treated as operator-verified public.

- **`relay`** · string · *reloads*

  `"on"` | `"off"` (default off): relay traffic for NATed members once this node has verified it is publicly reachable (or `advertise` is set). Announces the reserved `relay` tag.

- **`relay_client`** · string · *reloads*

  `"auto"` (default) | `"off"`: when NATed, register with up to two relay-tagged members and announce `relay:<id>` candidates.

## [compute]

<a id="compute"></a>

`[compute]` — parallel compute: how much memory the ephemeral object store may hold before it spills, how long an object outlives the job that made it, and whether the tail of a job is speculatively re-run.

**Read once, at startup.** This section used to claim it was hot-reloadable except the RAM budget; it is not, and an operator who edited `speculate` and sent SIGHUP got silence and no change. `SIGHUP` now says so out loud (`apply_config`). Making it true means putting the straggler policy behind the same kind of mutable holder `[limits]` uses, which is a change to how the executor reads it.

- **`object_ram_mb`** · integer · *restart*

  RAM budget in MB for ephemeral object bytes; beyond it, objects spill to disk. Absent = an eighth of system memory, between 64 MB and 2 GB. 0 = spill everything.

- **`placement`** · string · *reloads*

  `spread` (the default) or `pack` — how this node fills the mesh when it dispatches work.

  An unknown word falls back to `spread` **with a warning**, rather than refusing to start: the failure it guards against is a typo silently inverting every placement decision the node makes.

- **`object_ttl_mins`** · integer · *restart*

  How many minutes an object outlives its job's completion. Absent = 15. Long enough for a reduce or a `--out` fetch to arrive after the run reports done.

- **`speculate`** · boolean · *restart*

  Re-run the last stragglers of a parallel job elsewhere and take whichever copy finishes first. Absent = true.

- **`speculate_at`** · number · *restart*

  Fraction of a job that must be done before speculation starts. Absent = 0.95. Below it, an outstanding chunk is just work — unless there is no fresh work left to hand out, which opens the gate on its own.

- **`speculate_after_secs`** · integer · *restart*

  A chunk is never re-run before it has been outstanding this many seconds. Absent = 5. Raise it where a worker's first chunk pays a large one-off setup cost that should not be mistaken for a stall.

- **`uncollected_max_mb`** · integer · *restart*

  How much of a finished run's *uncollected* output this node holds past the ordinary object TTL, in MB. Absent = 4096.

  A result nobody has fetched is the answer, not an intermediate, and expiring it fifteen minutes after the run is how a transcode gets lost. Past this ceiling the oldest retained runs go back to the TTL and say so — pinning without a bound would turn a store with a ceiling into one without.

  Deliberately **not** derived from `object_ram_mb`: that is a RAM budget and results spill to disk, so a fraction of it would be the wrong size by orders of magnitude on exactly the machines that hold the most.

- **`stage_max_mb`** · integer · *restart*

  Largest total, in MB, that this node will **stage** to workers that cannot see the data themselves. Absent = 1024. 0 disables staging, and the run is refused with the mount named instead.

  Staging is right for a folder of videos and wrong for a dataset: the bytes cross the network once per item, and a ceiling is what keeps "meshware moved my files for me" from becoming "meshware saturated my uplink for an hour". Over it, the refusal names the ceiling as well as the mount, so both fixes are visible.

## [network]

<a id="network"></a>

`[network]` — what this node contributes to the port ledger.

- **`dynamic_ports`** · string · *reloads*

  The dynamic host-port range this node will allocate from: `"20000-32000"`. Absent = Nomad's default, and for Nomad's reason — above every registered service port, wide enough that exhaustion is not something an operator thinks about, and bounded so a node cannot be talked into binding something privileged.

  A malformed value advertises **no** range, which disqualifies this node from work that wants a port rather than silently substituting the default. A typo must not place a service somewhere its operator was trying to say something else about.

- **`reserved_ports`** · list of port numbers · *reloads*

  Host ports this node will never hand out, whatever the range says: `[22, 443, 5432]`. For whatever else is already listening on the machine and did not ask meshware's permission.

- **`dns`** · boolean · *restart*

  Answer `<service>.mesh` on this node. Absent = on.

  Every node holds the whole catalogue, so every node can answer authoritatively with no round trip — which is the property worth having and the reason this is on by default rather than a role some nodes take.

- **`dns_port`** · integer · *restart*

  The port the responder binds. Absent = 8600, Consul's, **not 53**: binding below 1024 needs `CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE` and this product's whole posture is that a node does not need root.

- **`dns_bind`** · string · *restart*

  The address it binds. Absent = `127.0.0.1`, which is the safe default: a resolver on this machine can reach it and the rest of the network cannot. Set `0.0.0.0` deliberately.

- **`advertise_interfaces`** · list of strings · *reloads*

  Interfaces mesh traffic belongs on: `["ib0"]`. Absent = every interface with a usable address.

  For the host that has more than one answer to "where is this machine": an HPC or GPU node with a management NIC holding the default route and a fast fabric the mesh should actually use, and a build host whose `docker0` and forty `veth`s are all real addresses that reach nothing.

  A name that matches no interface **warns and falls back to every interface** rather than advertising nothing: a typo here must not be a machine that silently cannot be dialed.

## [[volume]]

<a id="volume"></a>

`[[volume]]` — a directory this node lends to jobs.

Declared per node rather than centrally, because a host volume *is* a property of one host: the mesh has no way to know what is on a machine's disks, and a central declaration would be a claim nobody could verify.

- **`name`** · string · *reloads*

  The name a job claims it by. Becomes `MESHWARE_VOLUME_<NAME>`.

- **`path`** · string · *reloads*

  The directory on this node.

- **`read_only`** · boolean · *reloads*

  Refuse write claims entirely, whatever a job asks for. The operator's statement about the directory outranks the job's wish for it.

## [runtime]

<a id="runtime"></a>

`[runtime]` — how much of the machine the async runtime may use, how jobs are sandboxed, and which container and volume plugins to drive.

The default is every core, which is right for a dedicated node and wrong for a laptop that is also somebody's workstation. Both numbers are read once at startup: a thread pool cannot be resized under load without stalling exactly the work it exists to serve.

- **`worker_threads`** · integer · *restart*

  Async worker threads. Absent/0 = one per hardware thread.

- **`max_blocking_threads`** · integer · *restart*

  Ceiling on the blocking pool — the threads that run `spawn_blocking` work: redb commits, content hashing, filesystem walks. Absent = 512, tokio's default, which is a ceiling rather than a reservation.

- **`thread_stack_kb`** · integer · *restart*

  Per-thread stack size in KB. Absent = the platform default (2 MB on Linux). Lowering it is how a node with 64 workers keeps its virtual footprint sane on a small box.

- **`sandbox`** · string · *reloads*

  Per-job filesystem sandboxing with Landlock (`crate::sandbox`): `auto` (the default: sandbox where this machine can), `on` (refuse a job that cannot be sandboxed), `off`.

- **`sandbox_read`** · list of strings · *restart*

  Extra paths a sandboxed job may read and execute from.

- **`sandbox_write`** · list of strings · *restart*

  Extra paths a sandboxed job may also write.

- **`container_plugin`** · string · *reloads*

  An **override** for how this node runs containers.

  Absent is the ordinary case and the one to reach for first: meshnode detects podman or docker by itself and needs no configuration at all. This exists for the runtime nobody has written yet — gVisor, Firecracker, a hardened corporate wrapper — and it wins the resolution order when it is set.

  `meshnode` still links no OCI client: the static-musl, no-C, four-crate property is load-bearing. Driving a container CLI that is already on the machine costs nothing against it, which is what makes the built-in path possible at all.

- **`container_engine`** · string · *restart*

  Which container engine to prefer, when a machine has more than one.

  `podman` or `docker`. Absent means podman first — rootless, and no daemon to be down. This **reorders the search; it never restricts it**, because a preference that became an outage the day that engine stopped would be a worse setting than no setting.

- **`volume_plugin`** · string · *restart*

  The subprocess that provisions volumes on demand. Absent = this node lends only the `[[volume]]` blocks it was given, which is the default.

  Nomad's Dynamic Host Volume shape: the operation in `$1`, inputs in the environment, one JSON object on stdout. See `mesh_proto::volumes` for the contract and the two holes it closes.

- **`volume_plugin_config`** · string · *restart*

  Where that plugin is told to find its own configuration — the first of the two holes. Passed through as `MESHWARE_VOLUME_PLUGIN_CONFIG` and never read by meshware, which has no opinion about what a plugin needs to know.

## [history]

<a id="history"></a>

`[history]` — the local query index over jobs.

This is derived data: every fact in it also exists in the op-log, so the index can be deleted and rebuilt at any time. What it buys is answering "failed `deploy` jobs in the last 90 days" with a range scan instead of a walk over every job the mesh has ever run.

- **`enabled`** · boolean · *restart*

  Maintain the index. Absent = true. Turning it off leaves the node fully functional and makes `history` queries fall back to a scan.

- **`keep_days`** · integer · *restart*

  Prune indexed rows older than this many days. Absent = 0 = forever. The index is small (a few hundred bytes per job); the reason to cap it is a policy about how long history is kept, not disk pressure.

## [facts]

<a id="facts"></a>

`[facts]` — the fleet's self-description.

One setting, and it is **on** by default: collecting facts reads this machine's own `/etc/os-release` and `/proc`, which is the machine describing itself. A node that cannot say what it is cannot be selected, patched or diagnosed, and the bootstrap problem M18 solves by having a built-in collector comes straight back if the built-in one is off by default.

The switch exists for one real case: a mesh that still admits **pre-1.7 joiners**. Every fact publish is an op index a 1.6 build has no variant for, so a member that has published facts can no longer admit one. Turning collection off on the member that holds the invite keeps that door open.

- **`collect`** · string · *restart*

  `"on"` (default) | `"off"`: run the built-in `system` collector and any published collector whose selector matches this node.

## [sessions]

<a id="sessions"></a>

`[sessions]` — interactive terminals and forwards on this node: whether it accepts them, how many, for how long, and whether they are recorded.

Two settings, and both are bounds rather than features. A forward is a tunnel and tunnels grow, so the number one peer may hold at once is capped and the refusal names the cap. Recording a human's terminal is a policy decision an organisation makes, not a default a tool imposes, so it is off — and the *audit entry* is not optional and does not depend on it. Both are hot-reloadable (SIGHUP); a lowered cap refuses the next session rather than killing live ones.

- **`accept`** · string · *reloads*

  `"off"` (default) | `"on"`: accept terminals on this node at all.

  **Off is the default, and that is the whole security posture.** An agent you installed to run jobs does not silently become an agent somebody can get a prompt through; enabling it is a deliberate, local, auditable act. Turning it on is still not enough on its own — a session policy has to permit the user, and they still need the runner grant they would need to `meshnode run` here.

- **`max_per_peer`** · integer · *reloads*

  Concurrent sessions one peer may hold here. Default 8.

- **`record`** · string · *reloads*

  `"off"` (default) | `"on"`: write a transcript of every session to `<home>/sessions/<id>/`.

  Deliberately off, and not merely for storage. A terminal stream carries whatever was typed and printed — `export API_KEY=…`, the contents of a credentials file, a database dump — so a recording store is a secret store that nobody designed as one. The *audit entry* does not depend on this and is never optional.

- **`idle_timeout`** · string · *reloads*

  Close a terminal that has seen no traffic for this long. Default 30m. `"off"` disables it.

- **`max_duration`** · string · *reloads*

  Close a terminal this long after it opened, busy or not. Default 4h. `"off"` disables it.

- **`allow_root`** · string · *reloads*

  `"off"` (default) | `"on"`: permit a terminal when the daemon runs as uid 0.

  The packaged unit runs as an unprivileged `meshnode` user, so this changes nothing there. It exists for the case somebody runs `meshnode up` as root and would otherwise hand out root prompts without ever deciding to.

## [release]

<a id="release"></a>

`[release]` — where this node fetches its own signed binary from.

A fleet upgrade never hands a node a binary; each node fetches and verifies its own. That makes *where from* a per-node setting, and on a fleet of any size it needs to be a settable one: a thousand nodes each pulling twenty megabytes from GitHub is a bill and an outage waiting to happen, and an air-gapped fleet cannot reach it at all.

This is deliberately **not** replicated. A release source is a trust anchor — the place this machine will download an executable from — and a mesh-wide setting for it would mean one compromised admin could re-point every node's supply chain with one op. It stays where the machine's owner put it, in the machine's own config.

- **`base`** · string · *restart*

  Base URL releases are laid out under: `<base>/latest` holds the tag text, `<base>/<tag>/<artifact>` the binary and `<artifact>.minisig` its signature. Default: the project's GitHub releases.

- **`pubkey`** · string · *restart*

  Base64 minisign public key to verify against, if this fleet signs its own builds. Default: the key embedded in the binary.

## [state]

<a id="state"></a>

`[state]` — replicated-state retention.

**One knob, on purpose.** Retention is a horizon, not a size: an op is eligible to be dropped when it is *both* superseded by a later op of the same author *and* older than the horizon. A size cap would be a second knob that answers the same question worse — under pressure it drops the newest history first, which is the history anyone is actually asking about.

Not replicated, for the same reason `[release]` is not: it is a statement about this machine's disk. A mesh with mixed horizons converges perfectly well — each node vouches for its own holes — and the horizon each pass used rides on the checkpoint, so a mixed mesh is diagnosable from the log itself.

- **`compaction_horizon`** · string · *restart*

  How long a superseded op is kept anyway, e.g. `"30d"`. Absent = 30d. `"0s"` compacts as soon as an op is superseded, which is legal and almost never what anyone wants.

- **`compaction_enabled`** · boolean · *restart*

  Run compaction on a timer. Absent = true.

- **`op_rate_per_minute`** · integer · *restart*

  Ops a minute one *entity* may author on this node.

  Absent takes [`crate::backpressure::DEFAULT_ENTITY_OPS_PER_MINUTE`], which is set off the busiest legitimate writer in the tree and has a wide burst allowance on top. **`0` turns the limiter off.**

  The knob exists for one reason and it is worth naming: a control that can refuse legitimate work and cannot be adjusted is a control an operator routes around by other means, at 3 a.m., under pressure. If this mesh has a writer nobody anticipated, raising a number in a config file has to be the answer.

## [cache]

<a id="cache"></a>

`[cache]` — the action cache: whether this node serves and verifies results the mesh has already computed.

Not replicated, for the same reason `[state]` and `[release]` are not: every setting here is a statement about this machine's memory and this operator's paranoia. A mesh with mixed settings works — each node indexes its own shard, each node checks as often as it was told to — and the one figure that *must* agree, the epoch, is the one an operator sets deliberately on all of them when they mean to invalidate the world.

- **`enabled`** · boolean · *restart*

  Serve and publish cache entries. Absent = true. `false` still lets the node index other nodes' entries — it stops it *using* them, which is what somebody debugging a suspected cache bug wants.

- **`epoch`** · integer · *restart*

  Mesh-wide invalidation counter. Bump it on every node to make every entry ever produced stop matching, with no migration and no purge sweep. Absent = 0.

- **`verify_rate`** · number · *restart*

  Fraction of hits re-executed and compared. Absent = 0. `0.01` is the figure the milestone recommends: one percent of the cost of redundant execution, and enough to notice a systematic mismatch within a day on any busy mesh.

- **`max_entries`** · integer · *restart*

  Entries this node's directory shard holds before LRU eviction. Absent = 100_000.

- **`pin_lease_days`** · integer · *restart*

  Days this node keeps the bytes behind an entry it published, with nobody reading them. Absent = 7; floored at 1.

  Renewed on every read, so an entry people still hit never lapses. Raise it on a node whose cache is hit in bursts weeks apart; lower it on one whose disk is the scarce thing.

## [integrations]

<a id="integrations"></a>

`[integrations]` — governed egress: which hosts this machine may send data to.

One list and one match function, and it exists now rather than "later" for a reason worth stating: a sink is the easiest exfiltration channel in the product by construction — a text box that ships history anywhere, filled in by somebody who does not know what an allowlist is. Retrofitting a governance control **after** the first customer has a sink is how it ends up optional for ever.

Node-local rather than replicated, and deliberately so. It is the answer to *"what may this machine talk to"*, which is a fact about the machine and its network, not a mesh-wide policy — and it is checked on the exporting node **regardless of what any signed record says**. That asymmetry is the whole value: a signed sink is what the mesh agreed to, and this is what the machine will actually do.

- **`egress_allow`** · list of strings · *restart*

  Host patterns this node may send data to. Empty = no restriction, matching M15's specification.

  A pattern is a hostname, optionally with a leading `*.` wildcard: `warehouse.corp`, `*.internal`, `10.0.0.7`. Matched against the URL's host only — never the path — because a path-aware allowlist reads as more precise than it is and invites somebody to trust it for authorization.

- **`export_interval_secs`** · integer · *restart*

  How often this node looks for rows to export, in seconds.

  Thirty by default, which is the right answer for almost everybody: a sink is a copy of history, not a live feed, and polling a warehouse twice a second buys nothing but load. It is a knob because two real situations need it — a rate-limited destination that wants it *longer*, and a test that cannot afford to sleep through a real one.

- **`settle_secs`** · integer · *restart*

  How long a row must have been terminal before a sink sees it, in seconds.

  Five minutes by default, and the default is right for a real mesh: a run that finished elsewhere arrives whenever gossip gets round to it, and exporting behind the present turns "the row was late" into a non-event rather than a permanent hole in a compliance store. Zero is honest on a single-node mesh, which has nothing to converge with.

## [notify]

<a id="notify"></a>

`[notify]` — where "it finished" goes when somebody asked to be told (`meshnode run --notify`, `meshnode jobs wait --notify`).

Node-local, like `[integrations]`: it is a fact about *this* machine and the person sitting at it, not about the mesh. Nothing here fires unless a command asked for it.

- **`url`** · string · *restart*

  An HTTP(S) endpoint to POST to. An `ntfy` topic URL gets a plain-text message with a `Title` header; anything else gets one JSON object. Plain `http://` is allowed, because the usual destination is a self-hosted ntfy on the LAN.

- **`command`** · string · *restart*

  A command run with `sh -c`, with the event in `MESHWARE_NOTIFY_*` environment variables — for everything the URL shape cannot say.

- **`desktop`** · boolean · *restart*

  Also show a desktop notification (`notify-send`) when one can be shown. Absent = true: a person at a desk asked to be told.

## [disk]

<a id="disk"></a>

`[disk]` — the floor under everything this node stores.

**Node-local, and it has to be.** How much room a machine can spare is a fact about that machine: the build box with a 4 TB array and the ARM board with a 16 GB card are both legitimate members of one mesh, and a replicated number that suited either would be wrong for the other. This is the same reasoning `[retention]`'s node half rests on, applied to the resource that actually runs out.

What it governs is *meshware's own reclaimable data* — the content store, and job spools through the existing caps. It cannot make room that something else on the machine is using, and it does not try to: a node whose disk is full of somebody else's data warns and refuses to add to the problem, which is the honest thing to do and the whole of what is being promised.

- **`min_free_mb`** · integer · *reloads*

  Never let free space fall below this many MB. Absent = 2048.

- **`min_free_pct`** · integer · *reloads*

  Also keep this percentage of the filesystem free. Absent = 5.

  Capped internally at [`MAX_PCT_RESERVE_MB`] — five percent of a 4 TB array is 200 GB, which is not a safety margin, it is a disk nobody may use. The percentage exists to protect small volumes, where it is the number that scales correctly.

- **`warn_free_mb`** · integer · *reloads*

  Warn below this many MB free. Absent = twice the floor, so the warning always arrives before the reclaim does.

- **`reclaim_under_pressure`** · boolean · *reloads*

  Reclaim the content store when free space is under the floor. Absent = true. Setting it false keeps the warnings and stops the deleting — for an operator who would rather be told than helped.

- **`job_output_max_mb`** · integer · *reloads*

  The most output one job keeps per stream (stdout, stderr), in MB. Absent = 256; 0 = no limit. Past it the job keeps running and its output is read and dropped, with a line saying so.

## [git]

<a id="git"></a>

`[git]` — how this node runs `git` for a source it watches.

Node-local on purpose. A source record is signed by whoever added it and replicates everywhere; whether a machine will fetch code over a transport anyone on the path can rewrite, or run a commit nobody signed, is the decision of the person responsible for that machine.

- **`allow_plain`** · boolean · *restart*

  Fetch `http://` and `git://` sources. Absent = false: neither transport authenticates the server or protects the bytes, and what comes back is rolled out to every service the source bumps.

- **`require_signed`** · boolean · *restart*

  Ingest only a commit `git verify-commit` accepts, against the trust this account's git and GnuPG (or SSH allowed-signers) are configured with. Absent = false.

- **`timeout`** · string · *restart*

  Longest one `git` command may run before it is killed. Absent = 10m.

## [shutdown]

<a id="shutdown"></a>

`[shutdown]` — how long a stop waits for work already running.

`systemctl restart` is the documented package-upgrade path, and a restart that kills whatever happens to be running makes upgrading a thing operators schedule at 3am. The daemon instead stops accepting new work, lets what it already accepted finish, and only then goes down.

This is a *grace*, not a drain: it is bounded, it does not announce `draining` mesh-wide, and it does not move queued work to other nodes. `meshnode drain` remains the way to empty a node on purpose.

- **`grace_secs`** · integer · *restart*

  Seconds a stop waits for running jobs. Absent = 30; 0 = don't wait.

  Keep it under the unit's `TimeoutStopSec`, or systemd's SIGKILL arrives first and the grace was only a delay.
